tagline: Volcano islands where land diving began
overview:
Vanuatu is a Y-shaped chain of about 80 islands in the South Pacific, roughly 1,750 kilometers east of Australia and north of New Caledonia. Around 65 islands are inhabited, and the total land area is about 12,200 km², a little smaller than Connecticut, scattered over a long stretch of ocean.

About 320,000 people live here. Vanuatu has three official languages: Bislama, an expressive creole built largely from English words, plus English and French, and more than 100 local languages, giving it one of the highest numbers of languages per person on Earth. Port Vila, on Efate island, is the capital.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary republic. Most families grow yams, taro and kava and fish the reefs, while tourism and copra are the main exports. The country sits on the Ring of Fire, with active volcanoes, frequent earthquakes and some of the most damaging cyclones in the Pacific.
landAndNature: The islands are volcanic and steep, wrapped in rainforest and fringed with reef. Mount Yasur on Tanna is one of the world's most accessible active volcanoes: visitors can stand on the crater rim at night and watch it throw glowing rock into the air, as it has done almost continuously for centuries. Ambrym holds lava lakes, and underwater volcanoes rumble offshore. Cyclones can be severe; Cyclone Pam devastated the country in 2015. Coral reefs support turtles, dugongs and clouds of fish, and the coconut crab, the largest land arthropod in the world, can crack coconuts with its claws. Millipedes, flying foxes and the incubator bird, which buries its eggs in warm volcanic soil to hatch, live in the forests.
peopleAndCulture: Ni-Vanuatu society is organized by custom, called kastom, which governs land, ceremony and rank. On Pentecost island, men build tall wooden towers and dive head-first with only vines tied to their ankles, a yam-harvest ritual called naghol that inspired modern bungee jumping. Sand drawing, in which artists trace continuous patterns in sand to tell stories, is recognized by UNESCO. Kava, a drink made from a pepper plant root, is shared at dusk in quiet nakamal meeting places. Pigs with curved tusks are traditional wealth, and one appears on the flag. Laplap, grated root vegetable baked in leaves with coconut cream, is the national dish. Soccer and cricket are popular, and string bands play at village celebrations.
history: Lapita voyagers reached these islands about 3,000 years ago, and pottery and a burial site on Efate record their arrival. European contact began with Portuguese navigator Pedro Fernandes de Queirós in 1606, followed by James Cook, who named the group the New Hebrides in 1774. In the 1800s blackbirding ships took thousands of islanders to work on plantations in Australia and Fiji, often by force, and introduced diseases killed a large share of the population. From 1906 Britain and France governed the islands jointly in an unusual arrangement called a condominium, with two of nearly everything, including two police forces and two school systems. Independence came on July 30, 1980, and the country took the name Vanuatu, meaning roughly 'our land forever'.
funFacts: Bungee jumping was inspired by naghol, the Pentecost island ritual where men dive from towers with vines tied to their ankles.
Vanuatu has more languages per person than any other country, over 100 for about 320,000 people.
Mount Yasur has been erupting almost continuously for hundreds of years and can be visited on foot.
The coconut crab, found here, can grow a leg span of about a meter and climbs trees to cut down coconuts.
In Bislama, a helicopter is 'mixmaster blong Jesus' and a piano 'bigfala bokis we i gat waet tut mo blak tut'.
